sources.title: Stanley Kubrick -- orientation only (birth/death dates, citizenship, feature-film list and years, 1961 move to England, Look staff-photographer years); not used as support for any scored row. Fetched and read.

Stanley Kubrick (Q2001) -- identity verified live via the wbgetentities API: label 'Stanley Kubrick', description 'American filmmaker and photographer (1928-1999)', born 26 Jul 1928, died 7 Mar 1999, ko label '스탠리 큐브릭', P18 'Stanley Kubrick (1949 portrait by Phillip Harrington - cropped).jpg'. Orientation only.

Ed DiGiulio (president, Cinema Products Corp.), 'Two Special Lenses for Barry Lyndon', American Cinematographer (1976; issue date not stated on the page), mirrored on The Kubrick Site (visual-memory.co.uk) -- FIRSTHAND supplier's account (non-self for Kubrick; the author sells the equipment he describes) of the 1972-75 adaptation of a Zeiss f/0.7 lens to a Mitchell BNC, the 36.5 mm adapter, the 24 mm lens Kubrick rejected, the 20-to-1 zoom, push-processing of the whole film and Kubrick's stated reasons. The page's TLS certificate has expired, so it was fetched over plain HTTP with curl and read in full (page 1 of 1; pages 2-3 return 404).

Garrett Brown, 'The Steadicam and The Shining Revisited', American Cinematographer (original Aug 1980; revised 1 Mar 2022; theasc.com) -- FIRSTHAND operator's account (non-self) of the 1974 Kubrick telex about the Steadicam demonstration film, the sets designed for Steadicam use, take counts and framing demands, the 'harp test' variant, the rebuilt track and the year-long shoot. Fetched (whole article via WebFetch extraction); every passage cited was checked against the raw page text.

'Interviews with Colleagues' on The Kubrick Site (visual-memory.co.uk), excerpted from Michel Ciment, Kubrick (1982): interviews with producer James B. Harris (Cannes, May 1973), production designer Ken Adam, cinematographer John Alcott (London, Feb 1980) and Warner publicist Julian Senior (London, Feb 1980) -- four distinct FIRSTHAND colleague accounts (non-self) of Kubrick's preparation, sets, lighting, take practice, release and exhibition supervision. Ciment is the interviewer/compiler common to all four, so the page is counted conservatively as one source record although the speakers differ. TLS certificate expired; fetched over HTTP with curl and read in full.

Nick Pinkerton, 'Interview: James B. Harris (Part One)', Film Comment (undated on the page) -- FIRSTHAND account (non-self) by Kubrick's producing partner of the Harris-Kubrick company from 1955, the Brando/One-Eyed Jacks arrangement, Spartacus (Kirk Douglas asking to borrow Kubrick), Lolita's script and its UK production (economic incentive) and the Red Alert-to-Dr. Strangelove satire decision. Fetched; the passages cited were checked against the raw page text (a long interview, not every line read).

Sam Wigley, 'Producing The Shining: Jan Harlan on Kubrick', BFI, 31 Oct 2012 -- FIRSTHAND account by Kubrick's executive producer and brother-in-law (non-self): the Warner offer of The Shining, Kubrick's condition of writing what he wanted, and his agreeing to shorten the film for release outside the US ('He was not that stubborn'). All Harlan interviews and quotes (this, Sight and Sound, Zeiss) count as ONE perspective. Fetched and read in full.

Nick Wrigley, 'The right-hand man: Jan Harlan on Stanley Kubrick', Sight and Sound / BFI (published 2013, page shows 'Updated: 22 November 2019') -- Harlan on Traumnovelle (Warner contract 1970, postponed, revisited before The Shining, abandoned again, realized as Eyes Wide Shut), weekend home viewings, and 'Fast he was not - neither was Vermeer'. Same Harlan perspective as src_kubrick_harlan_bfi. Fetched; the interview text was read from the raw page (the Room 237 and exhibition sections were skimmed).

ZEISS press release, '(Probably) the most famous lens in the world comes back home', 21 Sep 2022 -- carries Jan Harlan's first-person recollection of how Kubrick learned of the Planar 0.7/50 in American Cinematographer, was told by Zeiss it could not be used on a motion-picture camera, and pursued the question; a company page re-telling Harlan, so the SAME Harlan perspective (and the same episode DiGiulio describes from his side). Fetched and read.

Kaleem Aftab, 'I'm Envisaging a New Kind of Movie: SFX Legend Douglas Trumbull on Kubrick, Malick and the Future of Film', Filmmaker Magazine, 28 Aug 2013 -- FIRSTHAND interview with the 2001 effects artist (non-self): Kubrick's command of technology, the moon-terrain disagreement ('agreed to disagree'), the Saturn-to-Jupiter switch and his backing of the spherical scanner. Fetched; the passages cited were checked against the raw page text; the Kodak perforation call is reported by Trumbull only as a 'legendary story' and is not used as a documented episode.

Scott Tennent, 'Full Metal Jacket Diary: A Q&A with Matthew Modine', LACMA Unframed, 4 Mar 2013 -- FIRSTHAND actor's interview (non-self): Kubrick's use of repetition to strip actors' posing, about two years in London on the shoot (stated in the interviewer's question and not disputed), Kubrick encouraging Modine's diary. Modine's remarks on Kubrick's temperament and his own family are not used. Fetched; the Q&A was read from the raw page text through the diary answers.

Thomas E. Brown, '2001's Pre- and Post-Premiere Edits', The Kubrick Site (undated) -- secondary research note quoting Kubrick's own remarks: 2001 opened 2 Apr 1968, early audiences and reviews were unfavourable, Kubrick and editor Ray Lovejoy re-cut it 5-9 Apr 1968 (about 19 minutes), and the helmetless airlock sequence was kept once published experiments suggested it was survivable. Quotes from Kubrick are self-reported; the perspective is the author's. TLS certificate expired; fetched over HTTP with curl; the premiere/trims section and Kubrick quotes were read, the shot-by-shot reconstruction of the trims was not used.

George D. DeMet, 'The Special Effects of 2001: A Space Odyssey', DFX (July 1999), reproduced on The 2001 Archive -- secondary retrospective: pre-production from mid-1965, consultants Ordway and Lange, the monolith models rejected, the corset-factory effects reel used to sell the film, the Slit Scan machine. Fetched; read from the raw page text (the closing effects paragraphs were skimmed). Quotes Kubrick's published remark on 'completely convincing' effects (self).

Fondation Napoleon page for Alison Castle (ed.), Stanley Kubrick's Napoleon: The Greatest Movie Never Made (Taschen, 2011) -- reproduces the PUBLISHER's blurb (promotional language): about two years of research, dozens of assistants, an Oxford Napoleon specialist, about 15,000 location photographs and 17,000 slides. Counted as one secondary/publisher perspective and only corroborating the firsthand Alcott account. Fetched and read.

Tim Greiving, 'From Kubrick to Spielberg: The Story of A.I.', The Ringer, 29 Jun 2021 -- long-form retrospective drawing on Aldiss, Ian Watson's essay, Sara Maitland, Jan Harlan and Bonnie Curtis: the Brian Aldiss story kindled in 1977, revived 1982, writers cycled through to 1995, the November 1993 announcement after Jurassic Park, and Harlan's statement that Kubrick believed Spielberg the better director for it. Secondary; Harlan's quote is the same Harlan perspective. Fetched; the passages cited were checked against the raw page text.

A J Black, 'Spartacus | Stanley Kubrick and the wrong Mann', Film Stories, 9 Sep 2024 -- secondary feature: Anthony Mann's replacement, Kubrick's requests on set (Rome extras, soundstages, a battle scene), his disputes with Douglas, Trumbo and Russell Metty, and his later remarks (to Gene D. Phillips and Charles Kohler) about decisions not being respected. The remarks are Kubrick's own (self); the author's claim that it was the last film without his control is one writer's characterization. Fetched; the Kubrick/Spartacus sections were read from the raw page text.

Sam Wigley, 'The letter from Stanley Kubrick that started 2001: A Space Odyssey', BFI, 3 Dec 2014 -- reproduces and describes Kubrick's late-March 1964 letter proposing a science-fiction collaboration with Arthur C. Clarke (three stated areas of interest), Clarke's 8 April reply and the 22 April 1964 Plaza Hotel meeting; letters courtesy of SK Film Archives LLC. The letter is Kubrick's own words (self); the dated action is what is used. Fetched and read in full.

perfectionism.rationale: [src_kubrick_brown_steadicam, src_kubrick_demet, src_kubrick_ciment_colleagues | 1965-68; 1978-80 | firsthand operator + secondary + firsthand cinematographer] Brown records about 30 takes of one lobby traveling shot on the first day of The Shining, Kubrick wanting 'at least two and preferably three perfect takes on each scene' and rebuilding a 300-foot plywood roadway three times for smoothness. DeMet reports the 2001 monolith rejected as a tetrahedron and as a three-ton lucite block before a sanded wooden slab was used, and Alcott (1980) says he often asks for many takes to get the most out of actors and was 'aiming for nothing less than perfection' on The Shining. Independent accounts from different productions converge; dual_edged because the same standard lengthened schedules (see execution_speed).

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_kubrick_ciment_colleagues, src_kubrick_brown_steadicam, src_kubrick_trumbull | 1971-80 | firsthand colleagues] Alcott (1980) says he 'makes endless notes which he gives to the technicians every morning' and wants answers by that evening; Senior (1980) describes a 30-page release 'memory jogger', checks of principal cinemas in France and Germany that found two thirds lacked a 1.66 mask (Kubrick's assistants then supplied them for Barry Lyndon), and a New York cinema's shiny white walls repainted matte black before the A Clockwork Orange opening. Brown adds a lens test with focus charts every inch out to 15 feet and cameras steady-tested nearly weekly, and Trumbull says his 'attention to detail and manner of working wasn't the norm'.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_kubrick_ciment_colleagues, src_kubrick_taschen_napoleon | 1964-71; 1980 | firsthand colleagues + publisher] Alcott (1980) says he 'foresees every eventuality a week or two before' shooting and tests in advance, and that his Napoleon research let him 'tell you virtually where Napoleon was every day of his life'; the Taschen publisher's note describes about two years of research behind the unmade screenplay. Adam says Kubrick had already worked for a year with NASA experts before 2001, and Senior recalls him collecting exhibition figures for every country over five months before a release.

execution_speed.rationale: [src_kubrick_harlan_ss, src_kubrick_2001edits, src_kubrick_brown_steadicam, src_kubrick_modine_lacma | 1964-68; 1978-80; 1985-86 | producer + secondary + firsthand crew] Harlan (2013): 'Fast he was not - neither was Vermeer'; it took him very long to decide, plan, prepare, film and edit, and some films were prepared and abandoned. Other accounts describe long schedules: 2001 took the better part of four years (T. E. Brown), The Shining about a year of shooting with framing still debated at the end (Brown), and the Modine interview puts the Full Metal Jacket shoot in London at about two years.

persistence.rationale: [src_kubrick_digiulio, src_kubrick_zeiss_harlan, src_kubrick_harlan_ss, src_kubrick_ringer_ai | 1972-75; 1970-99; 1977-99 | firsthand supplier + producer + secondary] When Zeiss said the f/0.7 lens could not be used on a motion-picture camera, Kubrick was 'not ready to take a no' (Harlan) and, in DiGiulio's words, 'persisted' until DiGiulio agreed to try; two independent witnesses describe the same episode. Harlan also says he returned to Traumnovelle after its 1970 Warner contract until it became Eyes Wide Shut, and The Ringer traces the A.I. story from 1977 through writers cycled to 1995 and the 1993 announcement. Some projects were also dropped (Harlan), so the score is not extreme.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_kubrick_digiulio, src_kubrick_ciment_colleagues, src_kubrick_harris_filmcomment, src_kubrick_filmstories_spartacus | 1960; 1971-80 | firsthand supplier + colleagues + secondary] DiGiulio (1976) says he liked to own all his equipment, even building his own location vehicle, and insisted a 20-to-1 zoom be built for him rather than rented; Senior (1980) says he supervised everything, including refusing a set stills photographer despite objections from Time and Newsweek; in Harris's account he could not continue with Brando 'dictating every step' on a Paramount western. After Spartacus he remarked that decisions may not be respected unless the contract says so (his own words, via Film Stories).

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_kubrick_harris_filmcomment, src_kubrick_ciment_colleagues, src_kubrick_trumbull | c.1962-63; 1973-75; 1965-66 | firsthand collaborators] In Harris's account Kubrick told him he and Terry Southern thought Red Alert would work better as satire, a turn Harris then thought would 'blow his whole career'. Adam (undated interview) says Kubrick was set against studio sets for Barry Lyndon and preferred painters such as Gainsborough and Hogarth as visual reference, against Adam's own conception, and Trumbull says he chose Bonestell-style peaks over Trumbull's lunar-photograph moon model. Dual_edged: Adam says the location shooting made the film very expensive.

experimentation.rationale: [src_kubrick_digiulio, src_kubrick_ciment_colleagues, src_kubrick_brown_steadicam, src_kubrick_trumbull | 1971-80; 1965-68 | firsthand collaborators] DiGiulio (1976) describes adapting a NASA-era f/0.7 still lens to a Mitchell BNC for Barry Lyndon's candlelit scenes, a 20-to-1 zoom, and push-developing the entire film one stop. Alcott (1980) says they tested a speeded-up sequence at two frames a second on A Clockwork Orange, and Brown says he devised a 'harp test' variation and designed sets around the Steadicam; Trumbull says Kubrick backed his spherical 'Jupiter machine' after painted Saturns failed.

curiosity.rationale: [src_kubrick_harlan_ss, src_kubrick_ciment_colleagues, src_kubrick_digiulio, src_kubrick_trumbull | 1960s-1990s | firsthand colleagues] Harlan describes weekend viewings of up to seven borrowed prints, many dropped after ten minutes; Harris (1973) says Kubrick's interest in nuclear weaponry led him to teach Harris about it before Dr. Strangelove and that he 'sees movie after movie'. DiGiulio says he taught himself every phase of technical use of his equipment, and Trumbull says he was determined to understand 'every lens, every camera'.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_kubrick_ciment_colleagues, src_kubrick_demet, src_kubrick_brown_steadicam | 1968-80 | firsthand colleagues + secondary] Senior (1980) says Kubrick, with days to go before the New York A Clockwork Orange opening, sent from London a list of Manhattan firms able to repaint a cinema, and once telexed MGM Australia a distribution budget for a 2001 reissue. Alcott says he found a way to hold an Arriflex almost like a Steadicam, DeMet says an effects reel shot in an abandoned New York corset factory was used to help sell 2001 to studio executives, and Brown says he had his own dailies projectors rebuilt to cure unsteadiness.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_kubrick_bfi_clarke, src_kubrick_brown_steadicam, src_kubrick_harris_filmcomment, src_kubrick_ciment_colleagues | 1955; 1964; 1971; 1974 | archive letter + firsthand collaborators] By late March 1964 he wrote to Arthur C. Clarke proposing a science-fiction collaboration with three areas of interest (BFI, letter is his own words); in 1974 he answered a Steadicam demonstration film by telex and later engaged Brown for The Shining (Brown). Harris says Kubrick asked for his help selling Killer's Kiss to TV, which led to their partnership, and Senior says Kubrick phoned him in November 1971 to work on the A Clockwork Orange release.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_kubrick_2001edits, src_kubrick_harlan_bfi, src_kubrick_ciment_colleagues, src_kubrick_brown_steadicam | 1968; 1980; 1973-75 | secondary + producer + firsthand colleagues] After the April 1968 premiere he re-cut 2001 with Ray Lovejoy on 5-9 April, cutting about 19 minutes (T. E. Brown, quoting him), and Harlan says he agreed to shorten The Shining after its reception ('He was not that stubborn'); Adam says Kubrick adopted his idea of an older house for Lady Lyndon, and Brown says Kubrick later admitted picking takes for performance rather than technical differences. Against this, Adam says he could not talk Kubrick out of location shooting, so the score is a moderate lean.

provenance.notes: QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities API call on 2026-09-18 for Q2001 returned label 'Stanley Kubrick', description 'American filmmaker and photographer (1928-1999)', born 26 Jul 1928, died 7 Mar 1999, ko label '스탠리 큐브릭' and P18 'Stanley Kubrick (1949 portrait by Phillip Harrington - cropped).jpg'; the assignment's search-hit QID was correct. Wikidata also lists a second citizenship (Q145, United Kingdom) that Wikipedia does not; nationalityCodes keeps US only, as assigned. SLUG CHECK: ls data-pipeline/candidates showed no stanley-kubrick file and grep of src/data/people/*.ts for 'kubrick' found nothing. CLASSIFICATION: occupation film_director only (photographer omitted: his Look photography is not the basis of any row); field film; regionCode north_america by birth and citizenship although he lived and worked in England from 1961 (the corpus has the reverse case, Hitchcock filed under western_europe) -- flagged for reviewer choice; era 20th_century. Tags perfectionist/detail_oriented/independent/innovator and archetypes creative_creator + independent_creator are each tied to scored rows. EVIDENCE READ: 17 source records (2 orientation, 15 substantive), all opened via WebFetch and/or curl; where noted in each title, the cited passages were checked against the raw page text rather than the whole page read. INDEPENDENT NON-SELF PERSPECTIVES: (1) Ed DiGiulio, American Cinematographer 1976, firsthand equipment supplier (he sells the equipment he describes); (2) Garrett Brown, American Cinematographer 1980, firsthand Steadicam operator; (3) Ciment 1982 colleague interviews on The Kubrick Site -- Harris (May 1973), Adam (undated), Alcott and Senior (Feb 1980) are four distinct firsthand speakers but share the compiler Ciment, so the page is counted conservatively as one source record; (4) James B. Harris, Film Comment (Pinkerton), firsthand producing partner (same speaker as the 1973 Harris interview in the Ciment excerpt, so Harris is one perspective across both records); (5) Jan Harlan (BFI 2012, Sight and Sound 2013, Zeiss 2022, and his quote in The Ringer) = ONE perspective across four records; (6) Douglas Trumbull, Filmmaker 2013, firsthand effects artist; (7) Matthew Modine, LACMA 2013, firsthand actor. Secondary or publisher records: T. E. Brown (2001 re-cut, quotes Kubrick), DeMet (DFX 1999), the Taschen blurb via Fondation Napoleon (promotional language), Greiving (The Ringer 2021), A J Black (Film Stories 2024), and BFI/Wigley 2014 (reproduces Kubrick's own 1964 letter = self). Kubrick's own words appear only inside those records and are never the sole support for a row. That gives at least 8 independent perspectives and 7 firsthand non-self behavioral sources; no row rests on Harlan alone or on one witness alone. BEHAVIOR-ONLY: rows are built from dated actions (takes, lens work, letters, telexes, re-cuts, release supervision), not from awards, box office or 'greatest director' reputation. EXCLUDED ON PURPOSE: fame, awards and box office; his fear of flying and 'recluse' narratives (health/anxiety speculation) and any private life or family matters (Modine's family story, Vitali's family); The Shining set accounts about Shelley Duvall (conflicting accounts, not read and not adjudicated); Kirk Douglas's memoir and Kubrick's own book-length interviews (Ciment, Phillips) except as quoted inside the records above; the Kodak-perforation call (Trumbull himself calls it a 'legendary story'); Modine's characterization of Kubrick as 'cruel'; Vitali material (the New Statesman piece was paywalled after its introduction, so it is not cited). Also read but not cited: Spectator/Zenou on Napoleon, Bookforum/Hamrah on Benson's Space Odyssey, and the parts of the Film Stories page beyond the Spartacus sections. CONFLICTS AND LIMITS: the f/0.7 lens episode is told by DiGiulio and by Harlan (two witnesses, one episode) and is used in persistence and, lightly, in experimentation only; the Senior cinema-repaint episode appears only in detail_orientation and resourcefulness; the Adam location-shooting dispute is used for independent_thinking and as counter-evidence in belief_updating. Harris says the Lolita UK production was decided 'based on economics' (a film incentive), so the 1961 move to England is NOT used as evidence of autonomy. Modine's two-year figure appears in the interviewer's question and is not disputed by him. The colleague accounts (Harris 1973; Alcott, Senior 1980) predate Full Metal Jacket and Eyes Wide Shut, so the late-career rows lean on Modine, Harlan and the Ringer account. RUBRIC BANDS: the 85+ scores (perfectionism 92, detail_orientation 90, planning_orientation 88, autonomy_need 90, experimentation 90) each rest on at least three independent documented accounts; execution_speed 16 rests on Harlan plus three separate schedule accounts; belief_updating is strong_inference at 0.56 with counter-evidence noted. PORTRAIT: LOC LOOK Magazine Photograph Collection photograph by Phillip Harrington, LOOK Job 49-U31 'Sadler's Wells Ballet', dated 1949 (added to Look's library 25 Oct 1949), reproduction number LC-DIG-ds-01160. The LOC catalog record (read through the public loc.gov JSON API; the HTML item page sits behind a bot check and was not bypassed) carries the subject heading 'Kubrick, Stanley', photographer 'Harrington, Phillip' and the item-level rights advisory 'Publication may be restricted. For information, see Phillip Harrington for Look Magazine'. That LOC statement (read on guides.loc.gov) says Cowles Communications transferred all of its copyrights in the LOOK collection to the United States, with a donor request that the photographs be 'Not to be used for advertising or trade purposes', and notes that copyright to photographs NOT produced by LOOK staff photographers may be retained by the photographer or heirs (a permissions contact for the Harrington family is listed). Harrington's own archive says he was a Look staff photographer by 1949 and Commons gives 1949-1971, so a 1949 Look-library photograph is treated as a Cowles-owned staff work covered by the transfer; RESIDUAL UNCERTAINTY: the archive also says 'on-and-off' and I could not read LOC's staff dates for him, so a reviewer may prefer to hold this portrait. The Commons file page (fetched; API extmetadata cross-checked) shows Public domain via {{PD-Look}} with the same LOC reasoning; its high-resolution copy was sourced via a Finnish news site (Iltalehti) from the LOC image and cropped from a 2049x1294 original. I downloaded the 1426x1140 cropped file and saved it as JPEG q85 with no upscaling (already under 1600 px); the saved file was viewed and is a single-subject 1949 portrait of a young man with a camera, with others blurred in the background. Kind is likeness (photograph from life). Rejected alternatives: 1963 and 1957 studio publicity photos (public domain only by a non-renewal claim), a 1944-45 school yearbook portrait (579x666), CC BY-SA 2006/2002 images (posters or artworks, not likenesses), two-person Look photos. KOREAN NAME: 스탠리 큐브릭 (Wikidata ko label; standard Korean rendering). The structural validator was run only after all rows were final; no row was changed in response to its output. PORTRAIT RIGHTS CAVEATS (kept out of the display license string, orchestrator edit 2026-09-18): the basis is the LOC LOOK Magazine Photograph Collection statement that Cowles Communications transferred all its copyrights in the collection to the United States, plus Commons {{PD-Look}}; the LOC item record carries the advisory 'Publication may be restricted', the Cowles donor request is 'not to be used for advertising or trade purposes' (this product does not use it for advertising), and the LOC statement notes copyright in non-staff photographs may remain with the photographer -- Harrington's staff status in 1949 could not be confirmed from LOC dates. The image is a 1949 Look job crop ('Sadler's Wells Ballet') showing Kubrick as a Look photographer.
